objections: Every retrieved item is off-domain: three identical World Bank indicator searches return only agricultural metrics (fertilizer consumption, arable land), and two OpenAlex searches return an NLP paper on sell-side reports (arXiv 2411.13813) and a 2015 Dieter Ernst paper on China/forging policy. Not one item contains an Intel financial figure, a consensus estimate, guidance, or segment data. Any directional lean on 'above consensus' is therefore refuted by total evidentiary absence — there is literally zero Intel-specific datum in the record, and the record itself flags all sub-questions [GAP: unprovable] or UNVERIFIED 0.00.

The same observed pattern — a research dossier assembled on this question — is fully explained by a retrieval-routing failure: full-question strings were piped as keyword searches into the World Bank indicator API (source=2) and OpenAlex fulltext.search, sources that structurally cannot hold analyst consensus or earnings data. Under that mechanism, whatever stance or confidence the pipeline attaches to the conclusion is noise from the query plumbing, not signal about Intel.

The two academic hits are keyword-coincidence matches ('analyst', 'earnings', 'consensus' in an NLP abstract; 'forging' matched to 'foundry' in the Ernst paper). A pipeline that ingests such near-miss documents as 'evidence' creates survivorship of lexically similar but substantively empty sources; repeated across many questions, this process manufactures apparent corroboration for arbitrary conclusions regardless of the true base rate of beats vs misses (~50% by chance for EPS).

The single most likely artifact: because consensus expectations are absent, any 'beat' determination reduces to a coin flip around the ~50% historical beat rate, so an affirmative answer would look correct roughly half the time purely by chance — and the SPECULATIVE 0.54 confidence scores sit almost exactly at that coin-flip level, indicating the pipeline's stated probability reflects default prior positioning in the absence of evidence rather than any information about Intel's next quarter.

The resolution date 2025-02-01 lies ~19 months before the evidence fetch timestamp of 2026-08-24T09:26:05Z, so this is a fully resolvable retrospective question about recorded exchange history, not an unprovable future event. The gap is a retrieval failure, not an epistemic one: querying the World Bank indicator API and OpenAlex full-text search for live BTC price observations was a tool-selection error, and 'no evidence retrieved' was then mislabeled 'unprovable' when the correct label is 'wrong sources queried'. Any downstream conclusion that the question cannot be settled is wrong.

All three World Bank evidence items carry the IDENTICAL sha256 (bd377215...) despite three different query URLs. Either the fetch layer deduplicated/cached responses without recording it, or the hash was computed over a constant wrapper rather than the payload. This makes the evidence provenance unreliable: you cannot establish that three independent searches were performed, so 'we searched and found nothing relevant' rests on at most one actual query, possibly corrupted by cache reuse keyed to the first request. The apparent thoroughness of four sub-questions each 'checked against evidence' collapses to a single bad retrieval pass.

The observed pattern (irrelevant agricultural indicators returned for every Bitcoin query) has a simpler mechanism than 'the question is unanswerable': the World Bank /indicator search endpoint matches indicator names/metadata only and ignores free-text semantics, returning a default page of source=2 indicators for ANY query string — note total:1498 is the full indicator count, unchanged across all three different searches. Zero signal here indicates a broken query interface, not absence of information. Concluding GAP:'unprovable' from a degenerate empty-result interface conflates 'the tool returned nothing' with 'nothing exists', which the OpenAlex items (count:113 for a Bitcoin-related full-text search) actively contradict.

Declaring UNVERIFIED from these two sources alone conflates retrieval failure with evidential absence.

The observed 'zero relevant results' pattern is produced by querying domains selected for guaranteed irrelevance (World Bank API for a spacecraft-return question) rather than by any property of the underlying fact. Any question routed through these two endpoints would return agricultural indicators and empty OpenAlex phrase matches identically — the pipeline would output 'no evidence' for the Apollo 11 landing or the current date. The pattern is fully explained by endpoint selection without bearing on the ground truth.

The single most likely artifact: the OpenAlex query in item [3] actually returned count=1, contradicting the summary's blanket claim that 'item [1] is an OpenAlex query with zero results' as if all scholarly search was exhausted. The one hit (a UBC library-science text) is irrelevant, but its existence shows the phrase-search methodology was near its noise floor, and a differently phrased fulltext.search or a title/abstract filter would plausibly surface the extensive 2024 CFT literature. Treating the evidence set as exhaustive is unsupported.

An alternative reading of the same record set: the identical sha256 hash bd377215dd... appears on all three World Bank fetches despite three distinct query strings, indicating the fetch layer cached or collapsed responses. If the fetch layer is returning canned/cached payloads keyed incorrectly, then the 'zero relevant evidence' outcome reflects a broken ingestion step, not a genuine survey of available evidence — the same mechanism would explain the empty OpenAlex results if their URLs were also mangled (the recorded OQL embeds the full question sentence verbatim, itself a sign of upstream prompt-leakage into query construction rather than deliberate search design).
